name: Blood Glucose Regulation
what: Explains how insulin and glucagon — produced by beta and alpha cells respectively in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas — maintain blood glucose levels within a normal range through opposing negative feedback loops.
why: Blood glucose regulation is a core case study in the study design and provides the physiological context for understanding type 1 diabetes and hypoglycaemia.

items.title: I can identify the two hormones involved in blood glucose regulation and their source
items.what: Insulin is produced by beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. Glucagon is produced by alpha cells in the same structure. The two hormones have opposing effects on blood glucose concentration.
items.why: Correctly identifying the source cells (alpha vs beta) is required for exam responses and is commonly tested.
items.example: After eating a meal, beta cells in the pancreas detect the rise in blood glucose and secrete insulin. During a long exercise session with no food intake, alpha cells detect the fall in blood glucose and secrete glucagon.

items.title: I can explain the role of insulin in blood glucose homeostasis
items.what: When blood glucose rises (e.g. after a meal), beta cells secrete insulin. Insulin promotes glucose uptake by liver, muscle, and fat cells. In liver and muscle, excess glucose is converted to glycogen for storage. This lowers blood glucose back to the set range.
items.why: Insulin's mechanism of action is directly tested in short-answer questions and is essential for understanding what goes wrong in type 1 diabetes.
items.example: Two hours after eating a meal containing 80g of carbohydrates, insulin secretion has facilitated glucose uptake by liver and muscle cells, converting the excess to glycogen, and blood glucose has returned to approximately 4–6 mmol/L.

items.title: I can explain the role of glucagon in blood glucose homeostasis
items.what: When blood glucose falls (e.g. during exercise or fasting), alpha cells secrete glucagon. Glucagon stimulates liver cells to break down glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis) and release it into the blood. This raises blood glucose back to the set range.
items.why: Glucagon is the counterpart to insulin and is required to explain the full negative feedback cycle for blood glucose.
items.example: After 6 hours without food, blood glucose has dropped, so alpha cells release glucagon, which signals the liver to break down glycogen stores into glucose, releasing it into the bloodstream to restore the normal range.

items.title: I can apply the stimulus-response model to blood glucose regulation using a diagram
items.what: A complete diagram includes both the high-glucose loop (stimulus: high glucose; receptor: beta cells; effector: liver/muscle/fat cells; response: glucose uptake and glycogen storage) and the low-glucose loop (stimulus: low glucose; receptor: alpha cells; effector: liver cells; response: glycogenolysis).
items.why: The study design requires students to use diagrams and the stimulus-response model to explain blood glucose regulation.
items.example: High blood glucose loop: blood glucose rises after a meal (stimulus) → beta cells detect this (receptor) → insulin secreted (control centre/effector signal) → liver converts glucose to glycogen (effector) → blood glucose falls back to set point (response).
